items.text: Can D(9), the ninth Dedekind number, be recomputed modulo small primes on INT8 tensor cores for far less than the published FP64 cost, within $1,000?
Switching Jäkel's matrix formula from FP64 to exact INT8/INT32 modular arithmetic cuts the cost per check enough that a few residues of D(9) fit in $1,000.
Each pair class needs a GEMM then trace; 4.26e9 pair classes total, but they are independent.
Interval classes and prime residues are independent sums, so 9,919 classes share one queue across 8 GPUs, and the matrices are built once and reused for every prime.
More compute buys more independent residue checks of D(9); at most about 5 primes fit, and 19 primes would rebuild D(9) exactly by Chinese remainder theorem.
One residue costs more than $750 (memory traffic and O(m²) work keep efficiency low), so the budget buys no full residue, only the measured cost curve.

Reimplement Jäkel's D(9) formula modulo small primes on INT8 tensor cores, benchmark against his FP64 path on one GPU, then spend up to $750 on 8 GPUs computing residues and compare each with the published value.
Jäkel computed D(9) with FP64 batched DGEMM on A100s in 5,311 GPU-hours [jakel]; Ootomo et al. emulate DGEMM on integer tensor cores [ootomo].

items.page_quote: There the matrices α and β are generated and multiplied. A batch of matrices is processed in parallel via CUDA's "cublasDgemmStridedBatched" kernel.

Content verified on the Jäkel page but the item cites no source. The page's algorithm does, per pair class [(a,b)], 'compute the matrix product γab = αab · βab; compute the trace of γab^2; multiply the trace with ω(a,b) and #[(a,b)]', then sums, so each pair class is an independent GEMM-then-trace. 4257682565 pair classes = 4.26e9 (and '4257682565 matrix multiplications'). Add [jakel] as the source.

items.page_quote: For D2 we compute 6, for D3 18, for D4 134 and for D5 9919 equivalence classes. Due to nauty's efficiency, the last computation can be performed within just a couple of seconds on a 2.4 GHz desktop PC. Note that according to Theorem 2 there are 7828354 intervals of D5.
items.note: 9,919 interval classes verified on the Jäkel page, and the page's algorithm is an outer sum 'for [I] ∈ Int(Dn)/≡' with each class's result multiplied by #[I], so interval classes are independent summands. The item cites no source for these facts. Prime-residue independence, the shared 8-GPU queue, and building matrices once for all primes are design choices the plan will build and need no source.

items.page_quote: 5311 GPU hours and 4257682565 matrix multiplications later, we got the following value for the ninth Dedekind number: 286386577668298411128469151667598498812366.
items.note: 'At most about 5 primes fit' is a cost prediction and needs no source. '19 primes would rebuild D(9) exactly by CRT' is a factual claim with no source and appears on no fetched page. Checked against the published value on the Jäkel page (D(9) ≈ 2.86e41): it holds only if the primes are the 19 largest below 256 (product ≈ 4.3e43, and 19 is exactly the minimum); the 19 smallest primes (≈ 7.9e24) or the 19 largest below 128 (≈ 5.4e35) do not suffice. The item does not say which primes.

Search on vetted statements is compute-bound with log-linear returns [seed15], but FATE-X may flatten because Mathlib coverage, not compute, binds.
FATE-X solved count keeps gaining about b problems per doubling up to the top budget, with no bend.
FATE-X solved count flattens (last two doublings each add under half of b) and failures show missing-library symptoms.

Run Leanstral 1.5 on FATE-H and FATE-X at token budgets doubling from 125k to 4M per problem on one 8x H100 node under $1,000. Check proofs with Comparator, calibrate on PutnamBench, and fit solved count against log budget [mistral].

scores.reason: Outcome decides whether to spend on INT8 residue runs, but D(9) is already known; value is a cost curve, not a pending choice.
Deterministic noise and held_fixed are fine, but the 1-19 prime axis exceeds the budget (about 5 primes), so the full span is not run.
Exact published D(9) residues and d(4)..d(8) serve as truth independent of the method, and small cases reproduce published numbers first.
Jäkel used FP64 and Ootomo emulates DGEMM; neither measures modular INT8 D(9) cost, and the gap is stated.
Pair classes were already independent; the plan lowers precision and regroups independent work, removing no sequential dependency.
Tuned FP64 cuBLAS path on same GPU and sample, exact anchor, p1b times both; baseline_copies is only vaguely stated.

critique.decides_by_reason: The decision rule needs measured cost per prime c1, which p1b benchmarks; p0 only counts classes and work, and p2 is the spend.
